blocks.text: Classification fine-tuning trains a model to assign an input to one or more categories from a fixed, known set of labels, a broad task family that the following topics in this module, sentiment analysis, intent classification, and topic classification, each specialize with their own domain-specific label sets.

This topic covers the general approaches to classification fine-tuning, the different classification problem types, and the evaluation practices that apply across the more specific classification tasks covered next in this module.
1. What Classification Fine-Tuning Targets
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472615531-967331015.png

Classification fine-tuning teaches a model to map an input, typically text, to one of a fixed set of categories, unlike open-ended generation tasks covered earlier in this module, the output space here is constrained and known in advance.
2. Generative Framing vs a Dedicated Classification Head

blocks.alt: Generative Framing vs a Dedicated Classification Head
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472615531-316915237.png

A language model can be fine-tuned for classification either by generating the label as text output, useful when reusing the same generative model across many tasks, or by adding a dedicated classification head, a small output layer producing a probability across the fixed label set, generally more efficient and precise when classification is the only task needed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Tradeoff"],"rows":[["Generative labeling","Reuses the same model interface as generation tasks, more flexible"],["Classification head","More efficient and precise for a dedicated classification task"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Structuring Classification Training Data
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472615532-574505354.png

Classification training data pairs each input example with its correct label from the fixed label set, the same basic shape used across sentiment, intent, and topic classification, all covered later in this module, with the specific label set changing based on the task.

blocks.text: 4. Binary, Multiclass, and Multilabel Classification
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472615532-45049404.png

Binary classification chooses between exactly two labels, multiclass classification chooses one label from three or more options, multilabel classification allows an example to receive more than one label simultaneously, the right framing depends entirely on whether the categories in a given task are mutually exclusive or can genuinely overlap.
5. The Class Imbalance Problem
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472615532-302369217.png

When some labels appear far more often than others in training data, a model can learn to lean toward predicting the majority class simply because it minimizes average training loss, techniques like class weighting, oversampling the minority class, or curating a more balanced dataset all help counter this bias.

blocks.title: Imbalance is easy to miss until evaluation reveals it
blocks.content: A model that always predicts the majority class can still show a deceptively high overall accuracy on an imbalanced dataset, checking per-class metrics rather than just aggregate accuracy is essential to catch this.

blocks.text: 6. Evaluation Metrics for Classification
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472615783-314794193.png

Beyond simple accuracy, precision and recall computed per class, combined into an F1 score, and a full confusion matrix showing exactly which classes get confused with which, give a much more complete picture of classification quality than accuracy alone, especially under class imbalance.
7. A Shared Approach Across Specialized Classification Tasks

blocks.alt: A Shared Approach Across Specialized Classification Tasks
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472615785-240171924.png

The sentiment analysis, intent classification, and topic classification topics covered next in this module all follow the general classification approach covered here, differing mainly in what the label set represents and what domain-specific considerations come with that particular label set.
8. When Fine-Tuning Beats Prompting for Classification

For classification tasks with a large volume of production requests, a fine-tuned classifier is typically faster and cheaper per request than prompting a general purpose model, since it requires no lengthy instruction or few-shot examples in the input, a practical consideration when classification runs at high volume.
9. Label Set Design Considerations

The quality of a classification label set itself matters, categories should be clearly distinguishable from each other with minimal ambiguity, an ambiguous or overlapping label set makes even a well trained model prone to inconsistent predictions regardless of how good the underlying fine-tuning was.
Worked Example

A team building a support ticket routing system needs to classify incoming tickets into one of six department categories. They discover their historical ticket data is heavily imbalanced, one department accounts for sixty percent of tickets.

Rather than training directly on this imbalanced distribution, they apply class weighting during training and evaluate using per-class precision and recall alongside a confusion matrix, catching that two specific departments were frequently confused with each other, a targeted review of the label definitions for those two categories resolves the ambiguity causing the confusion.
Common Mistakes

items: Evaluating a classifier with overall accuracy alone when class imbalance makes that metric misleading
Designing an ambiguous label set where categories overlap conceptually, causing inherent prediction inconsistency
Choosing generative label output for a high-volume production classifier when a dedicated classification head would be faster
Not checking a confusion matrix to see which specific classes are being mixed up, not just that some misclassification occurs

blocks.text: Practice

For a classification task you are familiar with, decide whether it is best framed as binary, multiclass, or multilabel, then sketch what per-class evaluation metrics, beyond simple accuracy, you would want to track to catch class imbalance issues early.
Key Takeaway

Classification fine-tuning maps inputs to a fixed label set using either generative labeling or a dedicated classification head, with binary, multiclass, and multilabel framings suited to different label structures, and reliable evaluation requires per-class precision, recall, and confusion matrix analysis rather than accuracy alone, forming the general foundation the sentiment, intent, and topic classification topics covered next in this module all build on.
